newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Victoria govt sees 97/98 underlying budget surplus.
newsitem.headline: Victoria govt sees 97/98 underlying budget surplus.

text.p: The government of the Australian state of Victoria on Tuesday forecast an underlying budget surplus of A$443.7 million for the fiscal year to June 30, 1998.

Announcing the state budget, Treasurer Alan Stockdale said the revised underlying outcome for 1996/97 was a surplus of A$802.7 million, compared to the government's September estimate for a deficit of A$700,000.
Including the A$4.2 billion contribution from the Victoria governments sell-off of electricity assets, the headline surplus for 1996/97 was A$5.03 billion.

"The budget is in sustainable surplus; we are improving service delivery performance and efficiency; we have lowered the public debt burden to levels on par with triple-A rated states; and we are rebuilding the state's infrastructure," the treasurer said in his budget speech.
Stockdale announced A$211 million in tax cuts, including a 0.75 percentage point cut in payroll tax to 6.25 percent which the government estimated would cost A$94 million in 1997/98.

"Dependent on continued sound budget outcomes, the government would expect to deliver further tax reform dividends to Victorians over the next four to five years," the treasurer said in his budget speech.
Earlier this month, Victorian premier Jeff Kennett announced that the state's diesel and petrol taxes would be cut by A$106 million.

Stockdale said the state's capacity to sustain tax reductions was limited by the underlying sustainable planning surplus, which it estimated to be A$126 million in 1997/98 and projected to average A$230 million over the following three years.

"Where growth taxes are reduced, the cost to the state revenue of the reduction grows over time. Against this outlook, tax reductions amounting to A$211 million in a full year are sustainable," Stockdale said.

The 1997/98 budget did not include proceeds from any further privitisations but the government said it would continue its micro-economic reform agenda with the privatisation of the state's electricity network, PowerNet Victoria and the restructuring of the state's gas industry.
Stockdale said the restoration of the state's AAA credit rating would lock in for the future the benefits of reduced borrowing margins.
Victoria's state debt is currently rated at AA by Standard & Poors Corp and Aa2 by Moody's Investor Service.

The budget's estimates included a forecast rate of inflation of 1.75 percent in 1997/98 compared to 1.25 percent in 1996/97, and unemployment falling to 8.5 perecnt from nine percent and employment growth rising to 1.75 percent from 1.5 percent.
Economic growth was forecast at 3.25 percent in 1997/98, up from a forecast 2.75 percent for 1996/97.
